# Introduction

## Objective
In modern supply chain management, late deliveries and unprofitable orders represent major operational losses. In technology companies an executive report stipulates that technology companies lose on average $1 million per logistics disruption/incident. This then leads to customer complaints, lost business and contracts. When supply chain disruptions occur on a large scale, restocking delays and high storage costs can lead to stockouts especially for goods intensive for delayed inputs. This project aims to analyze the extent at which both issues arise by building predictive models on historical logistics data. We will pursue and research these two primary learning tasks:

1. Classification (Supervised): Determine what predictors influence whether a shipment is at risk of delayed delivery (the binary target variable "Late_delivery_risk").
2. Regression (Supervised): Forecast the exact profit margin of an order ("Benefit per order") based on checkout-time transaction details.

Data Cleaning

Step 1: Missing value

```{r missing}
# Report missing counts and percentages
missing_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(dataset),
  Missing_Count = sapply(dataset, function(x) {
    sum(is.na(x) | trimws(as.character(x)) == "")
  }),
  Missing_Percent = sapply(dataset, function(x) {
    mean(is.na(x) | trimws(as.character(x)) == "") * 100
  })
)

missing_summary %>%
  arrange(desc(Missing_Percent))
```


```{r remove}
df <- dataset %>%
  select(-any_of(c(
    "Product Description",
    "Order Zipcode"
  )))
```
### Step 2: Duplicate:
```{r dups}
# Count exact duplicate rows
sum(duplicated(df))

# Inspect duplicate rows
df[duplicated(df), ]

# Remove exact duplicates
df <- df %>%
  distinct()
```
#### Step 3: Data Types
```{r datatype}
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    `Late_delivery_risk` = as.factor(Late_delivery_risk),

    `Customer Segment` = as.factor(`Customer Segment`),
    `Market` = as.factor(Market),
    `Order Region` = as.factor(`Order Region`),
    `Days for shipment (scheduled)` = as.numeric(`Days for shipment (scheduled)`),
    `Benefit per order` = as.numeric(`Benefit per order`),
    order_date = mdy_hm(`order date (DateOrders)`
    )
  )

str(df)
```
### Step 4. Unnecessary Variables
```{r var select}
unnecessary_vars <- c(  "Customer Email", "Customer Password", "Customer Fname", "Customer Lname", "Customer Street", "Product Image", "Product Description", "Product Status", "Delivery Status", "Days for shipping (real)")

df_clean <- df %>%

head(df_clean)
```

### Benefit per Order

```{r 3}

df_clean %>% 
  select(top_ten_cat, `Benefit per order`) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = top_ten_cat, names_to = "category_name", values_to = "category_value") %>% 
  # Group by category to find the total volume for slicing

```

## Analysis

### Validation Split

> "Approximately 75% of the observations will be used for training, while the remaining 25% of data will be reserved for testing. We also plan to use 5 Fold Cross Validation on this dataset"


```{r validation split}
set.seed(1)

train_idx <- sample(1:nrow(df_clean), size = round(0.75 * nrow(df_clean)))
train <- df_clean[train_idx, ]
test <- df_clean[-train_idx, ]
```



### Classification Regression (Method 1)

added in some of the top ten numerical predictors but didn't find anything useful outside of item profit ratio which didn't help

#### Response Variable: `Late_delivery_risk`

```{r logistic regression late delivery risk}

# inspect the number of n distinct rows for each column
df_clean %>% summarise(across(everything(), n_distinct))

# define usable categories (issues with the others)
usable_cat = c("Category Name", "Customer State", "Department Name", "Market", "Order Region", "Shipping Mode")
# all our selected predictors
# predictors = c(top_ten, top_ten_cat)

safe_top_ten_num <- paste0("`", top_ten, "`") # numerical predictors to fit on
safe_top_ten <- paste0("`", usable_cat, "`") # categorical predictors to fit on
top_sixteen <- c(safe_top_ten, safe_top_ten_num) # categorical + numerical predictors

# fit is adjusted to just include the numerical Order Profit Ratio as the rest didn't have high p-values
lm.fit <- glm(reformulate(c(safe_top_ten, safe_top_ten_num[8]), response="Late_delivery_risk"), data=train, family = binomial)
summary(lm.fit)
AIC(lm.fit)

log.probs <- predict(lm.fit, newdata=test, type="response")
log.preds <- ifelse(log.probs > 0.5, 1, 0)
log.cm <- confusionMatrix(data=as.factor(log.preds), ref=as.factor(test$Late_delivery_risk), positive = "1")
log.cm
hist(log.probs)
# calculate roc
roc_obj <- roc(response = as.factor(test$Late_delivery_risk), predictor = log.probs)

roc_curve <- function(roc_obj) {
  # simple plot is ugly
  # plot(roc_obj, print.auc = TRUE, main = "ROC Curve")
  # using ggplot for ROC curve
  ggroc(roc_obj, colour = "#2C3E50", size = 1.2, legacy.axes = TRUE) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
    annotate("text", x = 0.70, y = 0.25, 
             label = paste("AUC =", round(auc(roc_obj),2)), 
             size = 5, fontface = "bold", color = "#2C3E50") +
    labs(
      title = "ROC Curve",
      x = "False Positive Rate (1 - Specificity)",
      y = "True Positive Rate (Sensitivity)"
    ) +
    coord_equal() +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.border = element_rect(colour = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8)
    )
}

roc_curve(roc_obj)
# clean up memory so computer survives
rm(lm.fit)
```

 notice that the roc curve has these kinks / segments which is indicative of the categorical model dependent on a set of categories, instead of a continuous variable --> caused by only fitting on categorical variables, we didn't find our top ten variables to be useful for predicting `Late_delivery_risk`

#### Response Variable: `Benefit_per_order`

```{r log regression benefit per order}
lm.fit <- lm(reformulate(top_sixteen, response="`Benefit per order`"), data=train)
summary(lm.fit)
AIC(lm.fit)
summary(lm.fit)$adj.r.squared # Adjusted R^2

lm.preds <- predict(lm.fit, newdata=test, type="response")


eval_benefit_per_order <- function(preds) {
  lm.RMSE <- sqrt(mean((test$`Benefit per order` - preds)^2))
  paste("RMSE", lm.RMSE)
  
  lm.MAE <- mean(abs(test$`Benefit per order` - preds))
  paste("MAE", lm.MAE)
  return(list(rmse=lm.RMSE, mae=lm.MAE))
}
# out comes list of RMSE and MAE
lm.out <- eval_benefit_per_order(lm.preds)
lm.out$rmse
```

the fact that RMSE and MAE are so different is because we have significant outliers (not only in the predictors but also in the Benefit per order)

### Lasso Regression (Method 2)

```{r lasso regression late delivery risk}
library(glmnet)

x <- model.matrix(reformulate(safe_top_ten_num, response = "`Benefit per order`"), data = df_clean)[, -1]
y <- model.response(model.frame(reformulate(safe_top_ten_num, response = "`Benefit per order`"), data = df_clean))

cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1)
plot(cv_lasso)
# 5. View the optimal lambda values and non-zero coefficients
best_lambda <- cv_lasso$lambda.min
coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.min")

ridge.pred=predict(ridge.mod,s=4,newx=x[test,])
```


### Boosted Random Forest (Method 3)

```{r load}
library(gbm)
set.seed(1)
#fit boosted regression tree
#binary classification: distribution="bernoulli"
#regression: distribution="gaussian"
#more than two classes: "multinomial"
#n.trees: number of trees (default 100)
#interaction.depth=4 limits the depth of each tree (default 1)

boosted.rf.fit <- gbm(
  reformulate(safe_top_ten, response = "`Benefit per order`"), 
  data=df_clean,
  distribution="gaussian",
  n.trees=5000,
  interaction.depth=4)

```
